questions.question: What is the second posture in Bharatanatyam called?
questions.answer_text: The second posture is called Aramandi.

questions.question: In Aramandi, how are the heels positioned?

options.A: Far apart with toes pointing inward
options.B: Close to each other with a little bit of space and toes turned outward
options.C: One heel raised and one flat on the ground
options.D: Heels touching completely with toes pointing forward

questions.answer_text: In Aramandi, the dancer places heels close together with a little space and turns the toes in the opposite direction.

questions.question: What shape do the legs make in the Aramandi posture?
questions.answer_text: The dancer squats halfway down so the knees align with the toes, creating a diamond shape with the legs.

questions.question: What does the adavu series Thattadavu mean?
questions.answer_text: Thattadavu means striking steps. Thatta means to strike and adavu means step.

questions.question: What must the toes be in during Aramandi posture?

options.A: Pointed forward in the same direction
options.B: In the same line from one end to the other

questions.answer_text: In Aramandi, the toes must be in the same line from one end to the other.

questions.question: What does Thatta mean in Tamil?
questions.answer_text: Thatta means to strike in Tamil.

questions.question: In the Thattadavu adavu series, which postures are used as building blocks?
questions.answer_text: The Thattadavu uses Samapadam and Aramandi as building blocks.

questions.question: What is the key alignment requirement in the Aramandi posture?

options.A: The heels must be raised off the ground
options.B: The knees must be in alignment with the toes
options.C: The back must be curved forward
options.D: The arms must be raised above the head

questions.answer_text: The knees must be in alignment with the toes when squatting halfway down in Aramandi.

questions.question: How does the Aramandi posture physically differ from Samapadam?

options.A: In Aramandi, hands are raised above the head
options.B: Aramandi involves a half-squat with toes turned out forming a diamond shape, unlike the straight upright Samapadam
options.C: In Aramandi, only one leg is used
options.D: Aramandi uses only the arms; Samapadam uses only legs

questions.answer_text: Aramandi involves a half-squat with toes outward forming a diamond shape, contrasting with the upright feet-together stance of Samapadam.

questions.question: Why is maintaining the diamond shape throughout Aramandi so important?

options.A: It makes the dance look visually decorative only
options.B: It ensures proper alignment, strength, and balance needed for all Thattadavu steps
options.C: It is a superstition passed down from ancient gurus
options.D: It simply prevents the dancer from falling sideways

questions.answer_text: The diamond shape ensures proper alignment, strength, and balance throughout the posture — essential for executing all adavus built on Aramandi correctly.

questions.question: Describe the Aramandi posture in Bharatanatyam.
questions.reference_answer: In Aramandi, the dancer places the heels close to each other with a little space and turns out the toes in the opposite direction. The dancer squats halfway down so the knees are in alignment with the toes, forming a diamond shape with the legs.

questions.question: What is the Thattadavu adavu series and what does it involve?
questions.reference_answer: Thattadavu is an adavu series in Bharatanatyam. Thatta means to strike and adavu means step, so it is called striking steps. It uses Samapadam and Aramandi as building blocks.

questions.question: Explain how Samapadam and Aramandi work together as foundations for Thattadavu.
questions.reference_answer: Samapadam is the upright posture with feet together and body straight. Aramandi is the half-squat with diamond-shaped legs. Together they serve as building blocks of the Thattadavu adavu series, where the dancer transitions from Samapadam to Aramandi and strikes each foot rhythmically.

questions.question: Analyze the significance of proper physical alignment in Aramandi and how it connects to the larger discipline of Bharatanatyam.
questions.reference_answer: Aramandi requires precise alignment — toes turned outward, heels close, knees aligned with toes forming a diamond, hands on waist. This discipline ensures every adavu built on Aramandi is technically correct. In Bharatanatyam, alignment is functional: it maintains skeletal integrity, prevents injury, and ensures rhythmic accuracy. This reflects the art form's philosophy that mastery of fundamentals enables the highest artistic expression.

sequence_test.description: These questions test whether the learner understands the correct sequence of postures and adavus in Bharatanatyam.

questions.question: Which posture does a dancer learn first in Bharatanatyam?
questions.answer_text: Samapadam is the first posture every dancer learns.

questions.question: What is learned after Samapadam?
questions.answer_text: After Samapadam, the dancer learns Aramandi — the second posture with the diamond-shaped half-squat.

questions.question: Once two basic postures are learned, what is practiced next?

options.B: Thattadavu — the striking steps adavu series

questions.answer_text: After the two postures, the dancer practices Thattadavu — the striking steps series using both as building blocks.

questions.question: Which correctly shows the order of a beginner's journey in Bharatanatyam?
questions.answer_text: The correct order is Samapadam -> Aramandi -> Thattadavu.

questions.question: How does the Samapadam -> Aramandi -> Thattadavu progression reflect Bharatanatyam's teaching philosophy?

options.A: It shows that any random order of learning is acceptable
options.B: It demonstrates that mastering simpler foundational elements is essential before attempting more complex techniques
options.C: It proves that Thattadavu can be done without any postures
options.D: It shows that advanced steps are easier than basic postures

questions.answer_text: The progression reflects that in Bharatanatyam, mastering the simple before the complex is fundamental — each element builds on the previous with precision and discipline.
